newsitem.title: UK: British Labour leader pledges handgun ban bill.
newsitem.headline: British Labour leader pledges handgun ban bill.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party pledged on Tuesday to ban all handguns if it wins the next election as angry parents of children killed in a school shooting poured scorn on a government compromise.

Parliament voted on Monday to reject a total ban on handguns in the wake of the Dunblane massacre last March and backed government proposals allowing people to own .22 pistols provided they are kept in secure gun clubs.
The compromise decision will take some 80 per cent of legally-owned handguns out of circulation, giving Britain some of the most stringent gun laws in the world.
But several newspapers attacked the decision and Blair said he would strive to reverse it.
"If elected, we shall in the next parliament bring forward proposals...to amend this Bill to provide for a complete ban on handguns for general civilian use," he told the Independent newspaper.
Blair's Labour Party is some 20 points ahead of the ruling Conservatives in opinion polls with an election due by May 1997.
Monday's vote followed an emotional three-hour debate watched by a group of Dunblane parents, who shouted "shame" and burst into tears as the result was declared.

"The House of Commons brought shame on the nation last night," said Martyn Dunn, whose five-year-old daughter Charlotte was among the 17 people slaughtered in the Scottish village by crazed loner Thomas Hamilton.
The Sun, reflecting the mood of Britons -- 750,000 of whom have signed a petition for a handgun ban -- said the compromise "flies in the face of public opinion".

And the Daily Mirror printed a picture of Prime Minister John Major on its front page surrounded by 29 pupils of Dunblane Primary School who were killed or injured by Hamilton, with the headline: "He betrayed them all."
Urging members of parliament to vote for a total ban, rebel Conservative Robert Hughes said:
"If we leave handguns in the hands of private citizens, as regrettably the government proposals would do, we run the risk that once again we would have a tragedy caused by legally-held weapons."

Interior minister Michael Howard said the government proposals would protect the right of people to take part in the Olympic sport of target shooting while bringing in a much stricter gun control regime.

"If it is possible to provide the public with the protection they need and deserve while allowing some limited legitimate sporting activities to continue, it is the government's duty to take that course," Howard said.
